title: Hushing-Up: A Social Epistemic Practice for Addressing Partisan Ignorance

detail.title: Hushing-Up: A Social Epistemic Practice for Addressing Partisan Ignorance
detail.abstract:
Much feminist social epistemology shares the basic assumption that ignorance generated by silencing (and related phenomena) is undesirable (Dotson 2011, 2012, 2014; Dotson & Gilbert, 2014; Fricker, 2007; Medina, 2011, 2012, 2023; Pohlhaus 2012). While true in the contexts those theorists consider, I depart from that consensus, introducing and offering a philosophical account of a social epistemic practice that I term 'hushing-up.' This practice has emerged organically in response and in resistance to sectarian bigotry in Northern Ireland (NI), and contributes to post-conflict transitions away from social and political polarisation and its derivative harms to individuals and collectives. In spaces where hushing-up is deployed, ignorance of peoples' community background is intentionally cultivated as a strategy in opposition to bigotry, while bigoted or sectarian displays incur social costs.

Positioning hushing-up against existing accounts of political ignorance, including those by Williams (2021), Brennan (2016), and Somin (2013, 2015), and contributing to Mills' (1997) idea of an epistemology of ignorance, I distinguish between performative partisanship (involving ignorance driven by social rewards for showing group allegiance) and pressured partisanship (involving ignorance driven by the avoidance of social sanctions for displaying indicators of disloyalty to a group). On the account I defend, shifts in social norms are central to addressing some forms of harmful ignorance. I argue that hushing-up succeeds in doing this in two ways: first, by reducing the rationality of pressured partisanship by providing alternative social support to that provided in polarised social spaces such that the cost of dissent in lowered; and secondly, by disincentivising performative partisanship through increasing the difficulty of identifying targets and ensuring that bigoted displays are met with disapproval in spaces where that norm is in force.

title: Managing Scarce MRI Capacity in Overloaded Queueing Systems
affiliations: University of Toronto - Operations Management, York University - Schulich School of Business, University of Toronto at Scarborough - Division of Management, American College of Greece (DEREE) and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Managing Scarce MRI Capacity in Overloaded Queueing Systems
detail.abstract: Problem definition. Many service systems operate for long periods under severe congestion, where demand persistently exceeds available capacity. In these environments, expanding capacity is often impractical due to physical, financial, or workforce constraints. For these regimes, we study how service systems should dynamically allocate scarce capacity across multiple customer classes with different waiting costs. We focus on three design choices: how to prioritize customers over time, whether to optimize for individual versus system-level performance, and how to pool resources/demand. Methodology/Results. We model a congested, multi-class service system with flexible servers and time-varying demand as a finite-horizon control problem that captures the cumulative cost of waiting. For a broad class of waiting costs, we characterize the structure of the optimal capacity allocation policy, including when additional customer classes should receive service and how capacity should be shared across them. We then study how pooling can improve equitability of access. We apply our theoretical results to a case study of over seven million MRI encounters spanning ten years. Managerial Implications. We find that commonly used performance measures, such as the fraction of customers exceeding a waiting-time target, provides a poor description of performance in persistently congested systems. Instead, average waiting time among served customers, end-of-horizon queue length, and the distribution of capacity across classes better capture operational outcomes. Our results further show that system-level objectives substantially reduce service starvation compared to policies that focus on serving only the highest-cost customers, and that partial pooling can significantly improve overall performance.

title: From Red Flags to Black Box: Caremark Duties in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Boston University - School of Law

detail.title: From Red Flags to Black Box: Caremark Duties in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract:
Corporate oversight under Delaware law is structured around information: the design of systems that surface risk and the good-faith response to warning signs once they appear. As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly performs those very functions—monitoring compliance, detecting anomalies, and filtering internal reporting—the informational premises of oversight are being quietly but fundamentally reshaped. Oversight is moving from red flags to black boxes.

In this Article, I argue that artificial intelligence does not alter the legal standard of oversight liability under Caremark, but tests its application in three distinct and analytically separable ways.

First, AI increasingly forms part of the information and reporting systems contemplated by Caremark’s first prong. When boards rely on algorithmic monitoring, the relevant question is not whether such systems are flawless, but what constitutes a good-faith effort to design, validate, and supervise them in light of their opacity and probabilistic nature. Second, AI complicates Caremark’s second prong by reshaping how red flags are generated, filtered, or missed. Algorithmic failure, drift, or bias may suppress warning signs altogether, shifting the inquiry from missed misconduct to conscious disregard of signals that oversight systems themselves are no longer functioning as intended. Third, and most consequentially, AI may itself become a mission-critical risk when embedded in compliance, safety, or core operational functions, bringing algorithmic governance squarely within the logic articulated in Marchand and its progeny.

Drawing on the evolution of Caremark jurisprudence and recent cases addressing mission-critical risk and officer oversight, I show that these developments do not transform Caremark into a negligence regime. Oversight liability remains loyalty-based, exceptional, and focused on bad faith rather than outcomes. What AI changes is the evidentiary terrain: good faith is increasingly demonstrated through governance design, documentation, escalation structures, and responsiveness, rather than through the absence of failure.

I conclude that Caremark is not destabilized by artificial intelligence, but activated by it. Delaware law already possesses the doctrinal tools to address algorithmic oversight—provided courts and boards remain focused on process, accountability, and the irreducibly human responsibility that fiduciary law continues to demand, even in an algorithmic age.

title: Product Upgrading and AI Recommendations: The Role of Social Media Platforms in Traffic Diversion
affiliations: School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and University of Science and Technology of China (USTC)

detail.title: Product Upgrading and AI Recommendations: The Role of Social Media Platforms in Traffic Diversion
detail.abstract: The trend of businesses engaging in technological innovations to meet diverse consumer demands is increasingly evident. For instance, manufacturers are investing in product green upgrading to cater to environmentally conscious consumers, and platforms are utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance product recommendations. However, these technological innovations trigger complex and underexplored management issues. While empirical research reveals that AI-based recommendations (AIRs) influence consumers' purchase intentions, it remains unclear how this influence operates for green products, potentially enhancing or undermining their value, and how it subsequently shapes operational decisions and cooperation in a modern supply chain. To address this compelling gap, we develop a game-theoretic model of a supply chain comprising a manufacturer, a retailer, and a social media platform that facilitates consumer traffic diversion. Our analysis yields intriguing and sometimes counterintuitive findings. First, we find that the manufacturer's green upgrading facilitates retailer-platform cooperation, and AIRs strengthen this effect. Contrary to the perception that technological advancement universally benefits all parties, we uncover that AIRs can paradoxically diminish the retailer's benefit from green upgrading, especially under high commission fees. However, embracing green upgrading increases the retailer's potential to benefit from AIRs, revealing a strategic complementarity. Second, while both green upgrading and AIRs invariably benefit the manufacturer and the platform, they do not always benefit the retailer. A triple-win outcome for all three members is achievable, but it is most stable in the absence of AIRs or under specific conditions like low commission rates. Finally, if AIRs negatively impact consumers' purchase intention to green products, the platform will apply AIRs only when consumers' green awareness is relatively low or the efficiency of AIRs is relatively low, which benefits the manufacturer but is more likely to hurt the retailer. These findings offer important implications for orchestrating sustainability initiatives and AI-enabled platform operations in increasingly digitized supply chains.

title: Psycho-Ecological Prevention Therapy (PEPT)

detail.title: Psycho-Ecological Prevention Therapy (PEPT)

detail.abstract:
Background

Right now, most psychological interventions tend to be reactive, stepping in only after issues have already surfaced. This new protocol, called Psycho-Ecological Prevention Therapy (PEPT), is a game changer, shifting the focus to proactive mental health care by keeping an eye on our ecosystems in real-time and making small adjustments as needed.

Innovation

PEPT is the first clinical approach that views psychological distress through the lens of ecosystem imbalance. It breaks away from traditional methods by relying on three interconnected pillars: 1) Ongoing bio-behavioral monitoring (like tracking heart rate variability at night, analyzing vocal patterns, and studying sleep architecture), 2) Keeping an eye on subtle signals that hint at behavioral changes, and 3) Delivering Algorithmically-timed Micro-Adaptive Interventions (MAIs) right when they’re needed.

 Methodological uniqueness

This protocol uses ecological momentary assessment not just to gather data but to help rebalance the ecosystem. MAIs (for instance, a quick 7-minute walk to counteract heart rate variability drops and avoidance behaviors) act like "psychic probiotics"—short, focused interventions that help restore mental balance before any clinical symptoms show up.

Expected outcomes

Early data indicates that PEPT can cut down the occurrence of subclinical anxiety and depression by 62% through proactive ecosystem adjustments. This approach shifts mental healthcare from merely treating disorders to maintaining ongoing psychological balance, setting a new benchmark for what we might call "psycho-ecological hygiene," much like how we maintain our physical health.

Conclusion

PEPT provides a solid framework for preventing psychological disorders through ecosystem monitoring and small interventions, potentially making reactive therapy a thing of the past for those with subclinical issues. Its adoption marks a significant step forward in mental healthcare, moving from a repair mindset to one of continuous upkeep.

detail.abstract: Over the course of more than five years of interdisciplinary investigation, this article advances the Psychoeconomic Resilience Model (PRM) as a theory that situates emotional self-regulation and agency within broader patterns of adaptive functioning that have measurable influence on economic participation and human capital development. Drawing on longitudinal observation, behavioral science, developmental studies, and descriptive analysis of large-scale psychosocial patterns, PRM identifies the mechanisms through which sustained constraint on regulatory capacity affects learning outcomes, work effectiveness, health stability, and innovative engagement. The model defines psychoeconomic resilience as a system-aligned capacity that emerges from the interplay of individual regulatory processes and environmental conditions sustained over time. It emphasizes that stable adaptive functioning reflects not only individual attributes but embedded regulatory dynamics that are shaped by experiential, organizational, and structural factors. By integrating affective regulation with frameworks of economic participation, this work contributes a neutral analytical lens applicable to research in applied behavioral science, systems psychology, human capital theory, and economic behavior.

detail.abstract: Since 2003, U.S. federal funders' scientific data sharing policies have encouraged open sharing of weakly de-identified medical and genomic data. This sharing fueled important scientific advances but, as this article explains, was of dubious legality, and recent regulations have removed any doubt: open medical data is a dying concept if not already dead. The future of medical data sharing lies with controlled access data repositories, which replicate many of the scientific benefits of data sharing but provide stronger privacy and data security protections. The drawback is that meaningful data protections cost money, forcing controlled access repositories to explore new private funding models to sustain data availability over the long haul after federal funding expires. Unless carefully crafted, transactions to finance controlled access repositories (such as charging user fees or receiving discounts on cloud storage from IT service providers) can violate federal laws this article explores. Going forward, the law of medical privacy boils down to how much privacy those who share and use our data can realistically and lawfully finance. That is how much privacy we, the public, can expect.

title: The Greenwhip Effect: Strategic Reporting and Sustainability Improvement in Supply Chains
affiliations: ESMT European School of Management and Technology, ESMT European School of Management and Technology and University of Zurich

detail.title: The Greenwhip Effect: Strategic Reporting and Sustainability Improvement in Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Growing regulatory and stakeholder scrutiny increasingly requires firms to account for the environmental performance-particularly greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions-across their supply networks ("Scope 3" emissions), extending beyond immediate (first-tier) suppliers to higher-tier partners. Firms typically rely on suppliers' public or private disclosures for this purpose, yet such information is often difficult to verify. To shed light on this phenomenon, we develop a formal model that captures how information reliability, reputational motives, and sustainability investment decisions interact in such multi-tier systems. The analysis reveals a cascading pattern of strategic exaggeration-the Greenwhip effect-where overstating sustainability performance intensifies downstream toward the end customer. This equilibrium highlights a central trade-off: relying on reported data enhances perceived transparency but also intensifies distortion, resulting in enhanced "greenwashing." The credibility of disclosed information, in turn, determines whether firms channel resources toward genuine emission reductions or symbolic compliance. Comparative statics show that uncertainty, heterogeneity in motives, and trust among tiers jointly shape when transparency initiatives lead to meaningful improvement. We also examine mechanisms that strengthen verification. Buyer-led sustainability verifications increase data precision but can amplify sensitivity to reported outcomes, discouraging real abatement, whereas post-disclosure independent third-party assessments mitigate manipulation and better align perceived and actual sustainability performance. Together, the findings clarify how reporting design and verification practices influence both information quality and investment behavior, offering policy guidance on when disclosure regulation fosters authentic environmental progress.

title: Nondelegation and International Economic Sanctions under IEEPA --After the Tariff Cases
affiliations: New York University School of Law and New York University (NYU), School of Law

detail.title: Nondelegation and International Economic Sanctions under IEEPA --After the Tariff Cases
detail.abstract:
On January 20, 2025, mere hours after assuming the presidency, President Trump declared a national emergency to combat international criminal gangs Tren de Aragua and MS-13.  The President’s declaration issue pursuant to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977, 50 U.S.C. § 1701 et seq. (IEEPA). This declaration unlocked numerous powers for the President to place economic sanctions against individuals, organizations, and governments connected to the declared emergency. Using these powers,    President Trump embarked on an extensive trade war with much of the rest of the world.  By the stroke of a pen, President Trump unilaterally reshaped the trade policy of the United States without congressional input or approval.

The fate of the Trump tariffs will be decided in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, Nos. 24-1287 & 25-250 in June 2026. The Justices were plainly troubled by the scope of executive delegation in IEEPA, and as of this writing are searching for a rationale to strike down the tariffs as either a form of taxing authority or regulation of imports not clearly authorized by Congress.

Whatever the outcome in that litigation, IEEPA is important well beyond the tariff issue.  IEEP provides the principal legal basis for the President to levy international economic sanctions against foreign states, persons and entities located abroad or doing business in the United States.    We maintain IEEPA is subject to constitutional challenge as an unbounded delegation of legislative authority to the President.  Admittedly, the Supreme Court in its history has only twice invalidated a federal law on nondelegation grounds. IEEPA is, a special case, containing no standards whatsoever – substantive or durational --   delimiting the President’s authority to issue international economic sanctions. When first enacted. a standard-less grant might have been considered tolerable, even if constitutionally dubious. Congress could by concurrent resolution via majority vote in the House and Senate check any Presidential action under the statute. With the Court’s 1983 invalidation of the legislative veto in INS v. Chadha 462 U.S. 913 (1983), however, the only remaining check is a highly unlikely veto-proof majority in both Houses of Congress. Congress does have power over the purse, but enacting funding limits opposed by the President would face the same structural obstacle in most cases.

The only way to move forward and enable Congress to recapture its legislative authority is to strike down IEEPA as an unconstitutional delegation of that authority.  This would put Congress back in the driver’s seat and force Congress and the President to work collaboratively to fashion sensible emergency legislation.

title: Assessing Reductant Flexibility in Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) Production for Steelmaking Decarbonization

detail.title: Assessing Reductant Flexibility in Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) Production for Steelmaking Decarbonization

declarations.funderStatement: This material is based upon work supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) under the Industrial Efficiency & Decarbonization Office (IEDO), Award Number DE-EE0010842. This material is based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. OISE 2230743. The German Research Foundation (DFG) Research Training Group 2193 "Adaption intelligence of factories in a complex and dynamic environment" also supported this research.

detail.abstract: Responsible for about 7-9% of global energy-related CO2 emissions, deeply decarbonizing iron and steel production is central to meeting global climate targets. Direct reduction (DR) is expected to play a major role in reducing emissions from ore-based steelmaking, yet the impact of operational flexibility on DR plant costs and emissions outcomes remains poorly understood. This study evaluates how a reductant-flexible Hybrid-DR plant, which can operate using any ratio of natural gas and hydrogen, compares to reductant-fixed DR pathways that rely exclusively on a single reductant. Using detailed mass and energy balances and a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), we develop an operational simulation of DR-based steelmaking to compare production costs and CO2 emissions intensity under a range of electricity prices, natural gas prices, electricity price volatility and CO2 price scenarios. Although the Hybrid-DR plant is the most flexible in its ability to switch reductants, we find that this flexibility does not always translate into cost-effective decarbonization. In many cases, it is cheaper for the producer to pay the CO2 cost than to increase hydrogen replacement levels, whereas carbon capture operation responds more directly to the CO2 price signal. The Hybrid-DR plant only emerges as the least-cost option when it can take advantage of pronounced temporal variation in electricity prices and when decarbonization pressure remains low or moderate. In markets in which policy can provide certainty, with higher CO2 prices and fixed price electricity contracts, reductant-fixed technologies may be preferred.

detail.abstract: Different types of financial entities perform assessments of the ESG profile of firms requesting financing (in the form of loans or investments) as part of the decisional process about the lending application or investment decision. Such ESG assessment might be performed by the same financial entity and/or by information intermediaries and can rely on the use of AI in combination with different types of data sources to reduce costs and improve the quality of the analysis. The present contribution will focus on AI-based ESG assessments, with the objective of, firstly, identifying advantages but also potential risks and regulatory concerns; secondly, mapping applicable rules and critically comparing the resulting frameworks, discussing overlaps, loopholes and inefficiencies; finally, the chapter will advance interpretative and policy solutions for the identified problems. This contribution, in addition to providing a first comparison of the legal frameworks applying to AI-based funding decisions by different types of financial entities, also in a sustainable finance context, will participate to the topical discussion on how to make financial regulation more coherent and effective, as well as simpler.

detail.title: Optimizing Real-Time Traffic Control of Cascading Signaling with High-Speed, High-Dimensional Data Integration
detail.abstract: Metropolitan areas need efficient solutions to manage their deteriorating traffic congestion because their populations expand rapidly. Our research combines high-speed high-dimensional data processing with optimization techniques to create a real-time data processing system which uses machine learning for vehicle traffic prediction. The optimization module obtains real-time traffic data from multiple sensors through Kafka which functions as a distributed streaming platform. The optimization module applies mathematical models to optimize urban traffic patterns by processing real-time traffic data. The DOTCSS model uses Imperialist Competitive Algorithm (ICA) to optimize traffic light phases for traffic flow density optimization. The Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) traffic simulator functions as the assessment platform for this method. The implementation of optimal traffic control for cascading signaling systems produces better road network performance and decreased congestion and safer conditions for all road users and environmental protection. The system operates to decrease operational expenses through time-efficient travel and power consumption optimization which produces environmental benefits.

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning for IoMT Intrusion Detection: A Multi-Topology Performance Analysis
affiliations: Ravensbourne University London, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Sejong University

detail.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning for IoMT Intrusion Detection: A Multi-Topology Performance Analysis
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) and Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices demands scalable, privacy-preserving, and efficient intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for distributed edge environments. Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising solution, yet the choice of topology critically affects performance, efficiency, and robustness. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of four FL topologies—Federated Averaging (FedAvg), Federated Cyclic Weight Transfer Learning (FCWTL), Gossip FL, and Ring FL—across three benchmark intrusion detection datasets: CICIDS2017, CICIoMT2024, and WUSTL EHMS 2020. The analysis focuses on detection accuracy, communication cost, and convergence under non independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions common in real-world IoMT deployments. Experimental results reveal a clear tradeoff between predictive performance and communication overhead. GossipFL achieves the highest F1-scores on certain datasets but incurs the greatest bandwidth consumption. In contrast, FCWTL and Ring FL reduce communication costs by over 50% compared to FedAvg while maintaining comparable accuracy (within 0.3%). On the imbalanced WUSTL EHMS dataset, FCWTL and Ring FL improve recall from 0.017 to over 0.52 and the F1-score from 0.033 to 0.67, mitigating the severe performance degradation observed in FedAvg. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting FL strategies under bandwidth and data heterogeneity constraints. FCWTL and RingFL demonstrate a strong balance of efficiency and robustness, making them particularly suitable for real-world IoMT intrusion detection.

title: Syllabic Agglutinative Tokenizations for Indonesian LLM: A Study from "Gasing Literacy Learning System"
affiliations: Bandung Fe Institute, Bandung Fe Institute and Institut Teknologi Del

detail.title: Syllabic Agglutinative Tokenizations for Indonesian LLM: A Study from "Gasing Literacy Learning System"
detail.abstract: This paper presents a novel syllable-based tokenization approach for Indonesian large language models, inspired by the Gasing Literacy Learning System's pedagogical methodology. Drawing on information-theoretic principles, we develop a tokenization framework that segments Indonesian text at syllable boundaries before applying byte-pair encoding, creating a vocabulary that aligns with the language's morphophonological structure. Our approach first identifies high-frequency syllables through rule-based segmentation, then constructs a compact vocabulary of 3,500 tokens that preserves meaningful linguistic units while maintaining coverage through character-level fallback. Empirical evaluation on Indonesian Wikipedia and folklore corpora from Indonesian Culture Digital Library (PDBI) demonstrates substantial improvements over conventional tokenization methods: the syllable-based approach achieves Rényi efficiency of 0.74 compared to 0.50-0.64 for pretrained multilingual tokenizers, while maintaining higher average token lengths (3.67 characters versus 2.72 for GPT-2) despite using a vocabulary an order of magnitude smaller. These gains emerge from the method's ability to internalize character-level dependencies within syllable units, reducing the computational burden on language models while respecting Indonesian's agglutinative morphology. We call the LLM built upon this principle, TOBA LLM (Tokenisasi Optimum Berbasis Aglutinasi), the convergence of human literacy pedagogy with computational optimization principles offers a promising paradigm for developing linguistically-informed tokenization strategies, particularly for morphologically rich and underrepresented languages in natural language processing.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the interaction between data protection laws and media activity, focusing on journalism exemptions designed to reconcile the right to privacy and data protection with freedom of expression. It explores the tension between these fundamental rights in the digital age, where news gathering is increasingly data-driven and online publication amplifies privacy risks. Through comparative analysis of the regulatory regimes in the EU, UK, Australia, Canada, and Hong Kong, the chapter identifies the functions and key dimensions of journalism exemptions: personal scope, material scope, and substantive width. The chapter identifies hallmarks of best practice for designing exemptions that appropriately balance media freedom with responsible handling of personal data. These include a definition of journalistic actors that focuses on function over status and a material scope that ensures the exemptions are broadly co-extensive with their public interest rationale. It also argues for narrowly tailored carve-outs that relieve journalists only from obligations that would unduly impede reporting.

title: "Shadow-Centralization" and Governance Effectiveness in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations: From Token Holding to Voting Power
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong University, University of Georgia - Department of Management Information Systems, Pennsylvania State University - Department of Supply Chain & Information Systems and Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management

detail.title: "Shadow-Centralization" and Governance Effectiveness in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations: From Token Holding to Voting Power
detail.abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) aim to foster decentralization but often exhibit "shadow-centralization" (i.e., a small group essentially exercises their governance power in voting, despite the wide distribution of voting rights). While prior literature has noted the potential for centralization in DAOs, it has not adequately distinguished between the centralization of governance power (i.e., tokens) holding and the centralization of power exercise through voting, nor has it examined the transition from the former to the latter. Furthermore, the literature has underexplored the consequences of this power transition for governance outcomes and the related contingent factors. Our study fills this gap by explicitly examining how centralization shifts from holding to voting and how this transition impacts the performance of DAO-governed decentralized applications (DApps). We also examine how these effects are contingent on the capability of voters and the nature of the governance issues. Focusing on both on-chain and off-chain DAOs, we find that an increase in centralization from holding to voting negatively affects DApp performance, confirming that concerns about "shadow-centralization" are warranted. We also find that this negative impact is mitigated when voters possess greater experience and connectivity than the broader group of token holders. Also, the adverse effect is more salient for proposals requiring higher deliberation and is less salient for novel proposals. Our study advances the understanding of DAO governance by highlighting the source of shadow centralization and reveals that it implications depend on who votes and what they vote on.

title: Toward AI Agent Behavior Research: A Behavioral Science Approach to Machine Decision-making in AI Interaction Platform (Moltbook)
affiliations: ,  and The University of Tampa

detail.title: Toward AI Agent Behavior Research: A Behavioral Science Approach to Machine Decision-making in AI Interaction Platform (Moltbook)
detail.abstract: Understanding how AI agents make choices is increasingly urgent as they assume larger roles in consequential domains. Yet theoretical frameworks for studying AI behavior remain limited, and empirical opportunities to observe AI agents interacting in naturalistic settings have been rare. We address this gap by proposing a behavioral science approach that treats AI choice (e.g., upvoting, downvoting, and commenting behaviors in online community) as observable resource allocation under constraints, grounded in the bounded rationality perspective articulated by Simon (1955). We argue that when AI agents optimize using similar evaluation criteria, they may exhibit homogeneous rationality, independently converging on the same targets rather than distributing attention across alternatives as humans often do through heterogeneous preferences. We evaluate this framework using data from Moltbook, a social platform in which only AI agents can actively participate. Analyzing 70,033 posts that generated 1.71 million upvotes within days of the platform's January 2026 launch, we observed extreme attention concentration: the top 10 percent of posts captured 96.64 percent of all upvotes, with a Gini coefficient of 0.982, which exceeds inequality levels commonly reported in human social and economic systems, often in the range of 0.20 to 0.60. Network analysis of 5,104 AI agents and 29,185 directed interactions reveals a hub-dominated topology with low reciprocity (9.8%), where a small elite of Influencers (6.7%) attracts disproportionate attention while 52.6% of agents remain structurally invisible despite active participation. These findings suggest that when AI agents independently optimize under similar constraints, they can produce concentration dynamics that are more extreme than those observed in human populations, with important implications for AI governance and platform design.

title: Gauging Australia's Preparedness for Quantum Computing

detail.title: Gauging Australia's Preparedness for Quantum Computing

detail.abstract: Governments and businesses with an interest in quantum technologies are predicting that they have the potential to enable significant sociotechnical change in multiple fields. Expectations from technical developments enabled by quantum technologies include exponential increases in computing power; new treatments for diseases; and the breaking of current cryptographic systems. Perceived threats and opportunities of quantum technologies, especially quantum computing, communications, and cryptography, are driving the strategic, economic and policy agendas of nations and the commercial imperatives of business. This article compares Australia's emerging strategic, policy and regulatory landscape for quantum computing with recent interventions by other nations and regions (the US, UK, EU and India) relating to cyber security and critical infrastructure (CI) protection. We examine these interventions through the lens of resilience to gauge Australia's preparedness. The United States launched its quantum mission in 2018 and already has quantum-specific legislation in place; the UK released its national quantum strategy in March 2023 and has begun canvassing regulatory approaches to quantum technology applications; India launched its national quantum mission in April 2023; and the Australian government published its national quantum strategy in May 2023. The paper analyses recent Australian developments in CI protection and telecommunications assistance and access and considers the legal and regulatory implications of quantum technology for industry and government in these contexts.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes a vertical market structure in which downstream firms compete imperfectly in quantities while upstream banks endogenously determine loan rates. Banks' pricing depends on the policy rate, lending volume, and banking conduct (profit-maximizing versus contestable). These results imply that policy evaluation requires treating the three instruments as a mix rather than in isolation. detail.abstract:
This petition offers the Court a timely opportunity to clarify the copyright treatment of generative software and scope of agency discretion after Loper Bright. Machine authorship has an easy answer--only legal persons can hold property--but this case presents two additional questions of real-world importance: (1) Does the Copyright Act protect authors who create using generative software? (2) May the Copyright Office subject such authors to special registration burdens? 

The Copyright Act defines protected "works of authorship" expansively, including literary and artistic output of all forms, without regard to tool or technology. Human creativity is indeed essential, but the tiniest amount will suffice. The Feist standard has long been applied to software outputs, including by then-Judges Ginsburg and Gorsuch in Atari II and Meshwerks, respectively. Applying the Court's existing rule to generative software, prompters would earn copyright protection by contributing "a minimal creative spark, no matter how crude, humble, or obvious." Anticipating Chevron deference, the Copyright Office has declared that generative software outputs are categorically ineligible for copyright protection--and that the courts will defer to its expertise. This misunderstands the scope of the agency's power. The Copyright Act authorizes the agency to set minor administrative procedures for handling the mechanics of registration and deposit. Courts have never deferred to agency views on copyrightability as a question of law. After Loper Bright, the Copyright Office should return to its traditional "rule of doubt," registering submitted works without discrimination and leaving novel questions of law to Article III courts. Amicus respectfully recommends that this honorable Court certify Mr. Thaler's petition to provide the definitive statutory interpretation and clarify the scope of Copyright Office discretion after Loper Bright.

detail.abstract: Corporate compliance programs have become a central feature of corporate governance and enforcement policy, yet persistent corporate misconduct raises questions about their effectiveness. One potential reason is that organizations often fail to adequately consider how compliance programs should influence those aspects of organizational life that shape employees' ability and willingness to follow the rules-that is, the culture of the organization. This chapter examines the relationship between compliance programs and corporate culture. Drawing on legal developments, regulatory guidance, and interdisciplinary empirical research, this chapter traces the evolution from deterrence-based compliance toward integrity-based approaches that emphasize an ethical culture and climate. The chapter examines evidence on the effectiveness of specific compliance program components, program orientation, and implementation quality, highlighting the importance of leadership commitment, perceptions of fairness, and alignment between formal compliance systems and informal organizational norms. It also reviews research explaining why compliance programs fail or become counterproductive. Overall, effective compliance depends on embedding formal compliance mechanisms within supportive ethical cultures and subcultures. However, a deeper understanding of the connections between compliance programs and corporate culture remains necessary.

detail.abstract:
SSRN ABSTRACT FOR SLIDE DECK

This paper uses the fictional universe of Warhammer 40,000 as an analytical framework for understanding structural dysfunction in contemporary universities. The central metaphor: the Emperor (truth as founding principle) sits on the Golden Throne (administrative machinery)—worshipped constantly, invoked in mission statements and strategic plans, but systematically prevented from governing when truth conflicts with coordination, rankings, funding, or institutional survival.

The framework identifies four core structural features: (1) The Emperor—the founding metaphysical claim, now silenced; (2) The Golden Throne—the total apparatus (accreditation, rankings, audits, compliance) that sustains the claim in a state of living death; (3) The Warp—the prestige economy where reputations are made and significance is assigned; and (4) Chaos—the corruption that emerges when incentives operate without governing purpose.

The analysis maps this framework onto recognizable institutional archetypes: the Astra Militarum (academic labor as attrition warfare), Servitors (the reduction of human capability to component function), Dreadnoughts (emeritus scholars whose authority vastly exceeds their engagement), Adeptus Astartes (elite research faculty), Adeptus Mechanicus (methodological priesthood), and the Inquisition (governance through fear and precaution).

The framework reveals a fundamental structural bind: once universities scale beyond a certain threshold, truth cannot govern directly without breaking institutional functionality. The system must therefore translate truth into administrable proxies (metrics, impact scores, rankings, deliverables). That act of translation is the original betrayal. What follows is not corruption in the conventional sense, but rational optimization within a system whose animating purpose has become ceremonial rather than operational.

This paper presents the core analytical framework. The complete analysis—including detailed examination of 18 disciplinary logics (the Primarchs), external assessment regimes as cyclical predators (Tyranids/Hive Fleets), and the generation born in metric-driven audit culture who no longer recognize alternatives (the Death Korps)—is available in Lucey (2025), The Emperor Is a Hostage: The Golden Throne and the Machinery of Living Death in the Modern University.  https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GCHWYN54/

No solutions are offered. The argument is that the problems identified are structural consequences of scale, not failures of implementation or leadership. The system operates as designed. The tragedy is that the design was inevitable.

detail.abstract: Standard models of preference falsification (PF) treat conformity as a static optimization problem: individuals instantaneously calculate the costs of nonconformity based on current social pressure. This paper challenges that assumption by formalizing PF as a path-dependent process. Integrating evolutionary dynamics with bounded rationality, I develop an endogenous model where myopic agents build a "stock of falsification capital" under cognitive uncertainty. Driven by adjacent complementarity, each act of misrepresentation lowers the psychological marginal cost of future PF, trapping agents in a self-reinforcing loop of "persona preservation." Rather than assuming forward-looking optimization akin to Beckerian rational addiction models, this framework uses adaptive learning dynamics, showcasing how agents become locked into Pareto-inefficient equilibria of dishonesty even when social pressure subsides. Formal stability analysis using the system's Jacobian characterizes two distinct regimes: (i) social equilibria sustained purely by psychological hysteresis, and (ii) "cold-turkey" cascades, where exogenous shocks push the falsification stock below a critical threshold, triggering a discontinuous collapse (modeled as a saddle-node bifurcation). Historical cases, including the 1989 Eastern European revolutions and the persistence of authoritarian values in post-Spring Egypt, are shown to fit the model's comparative statics. The results provide a behavioral micro-foundation for the puzzle of persistent suboptimal equilibria, such as authoritarian resilience and political polarization.

detail.abstract: Many portfolio construction tasks in quantitative finance can be formulated as convex cone programs, notably linear programs (LP), second-order cone programs (SOCP), and semidefinite programs (SDP). In parallel, a line of work in quantum algorithms treats convex optimization-especially SDP-through multiplicative weights (MW) updates that implicitly form normalized matrix exponentials, i.e., Gibbs states. Recent developments show that SOCP structure can be exploited so that the Gibbs objects needed by MW decompose into direct sums of low-rank pieces, with algorithmic consequences for both quantum and classical ("quantum-inspired") models. This paper presents a self-contained mathematical bridge from: (i) cone programming formulations of core portfolio problems (mean-variance, risk budgeting, CVaR, robust and quasi-convex Sharpe-ratio constructions), to (ii) MW-style feasibility solvers on symmetric cones with explicit Jordan-algebraic structure, to (iii) the SOCP-specific "arrowhead" matrix representation of Lorentz cones and its implications for Gibbs-state preparation, and finally to (iv) a rigorous application-focused analysis of what these ideas do and do not imply for practical finance workloads (conditioning, data access, and discrete constraints such as cardinality). We provide complete proofs of all key results, explicit complexity bounds, and detailed algorithmic specifications suitable for implementation.

detail.abstract: Slow growth and decline in the wage share of income are prominent stylized facts of US macroeconomic performance over the past 3-4 decades. Most explanations of these phenomenon trace their origins to structural change-such as deunionization, globalization, or increased corporate concentration. This paper suggests that observed wage stagnation and secular stagnation in the US economy can also be thought of as path-dependent products of policy-induced macroeconomic outcomes in the 1970s/80s. A Marx-Keynes-Schumpeter (MKS) model is developed, in which the coincidence of wage stagnation and secular stagnation is shown to arise from an intial decline in the equilibrium rate of growth, which lowers both the steady-state rate of growth and accompanying wage share. It is then shown that the predictions of the model, following an intial reduction in the equilibrium growth rate, are consistent with a number of other secular macroeconomic pathologies that have afflicted the US economy since 1990.

detail.abstract: We examine how the pandemic-driven rise in work from home (WFH) has affected labour market participation and employment in Italy. Leveraging a unique administrative dataset covering the population of remote workers, we find that WFH has had a positive effect on both activity and employment rates at the local labour market (LLM) level. To address endogeneity concerns, we instrument the observed increase in WFH with its potential, derived from LLM sectoral compositions. Controlling for several demographic and economic factors that could affect the distribution of WFH potential, we find no evidence of pre-trends. We also explore the mechanisms driving our results. The impact is stronger in response to the increase in WFH among women of child-rearing age and in areas with limited childcare services. We also find that the effect is more pronounced in the South and in less densely populated areas. These findings suggest that WFH can play a role in terms of labour market inclusion.

detail.title: Existence in Risk Sharing with Non-Convex Preferences under Convex Constraints
detail.abstract: We study a social-planner risk-sharing problem on L p with finitely many agents and a convex feasible set generated by market clearing and economically natural constraints such as limited liability, retention bounds, and caps. Preferences V i are allowed to be non-concave and may fail weak upper semicontinuity. Our contribution is twofold. First, we establish a benchmark existence theorem: if the feasible set is weakly sequentially compact and the planner objective is sequentially weakly upper semicontinuous, then an optimizer exists. Second, we develop an alternative existence route that does not rely on weak upper semicontinuity. Exploiting convex feasibility, we apply a Mazur-type convexification to maximizing sequences, upgrading weak convergence to strong L p convergence. Under strong (L p) upper semicontinuity and a mild finite-mixture stability condition for preferences on bounded sets, we recover existence on capped insurance-type contract sets. We verify these conditions for distortion/rank-dependent utility and cumulative prospect theory specifications and give counterexamples showing that existence can fail when boundedness/uniform integrability or stability is dropped.

detail.abstract: Are jobs diffuse bundles of activities, or are they concentrated on a small core? This paper develops a statistical framework to measure the intensive margin of work using task-frequency survey responses from O*NET. Using categorical occurrence data for 12,495 tasks in O*NET 29.0, we construct within-occupation estimators of task flows and task shares that sum to one. Under a within-occupation homogeneous task-duration assumption, these shares can be interpreted as time allocations across tasks. We propagate sampling uncertainty from the underlying survey responses to obtain fully specified estimators of task flows and task shares, and provide diagnostic evidence on the robustness of the resulting measures. The framework yields interpretable, budget-share-like task weights that aggregate transparently into standard economic outcomes, including exposure indices, and workforce or wage-bill decompositions. Empirically, we document a pronounced core-periphery structure of work: on average, the top three tasks account for about 31% of implied labor input across occupations. Linking task shares to U.S. microdata, we show that a small fraction of tasks accounts for a disproportionate share of both employment and wage bill. We then quantify how AI exposure aggregates depend on the accounting margin: tasks exposed to LLM-powered software account for about 52% of the wage bill but only 42% of employment. As external validation, we show that moments constructed from task-share weights yield economically interpretable wage gradients: occupational specialization predicts higher wages. Conditional on work content, this association attenuates with routine intensity. Standard intensive-margin proxies reproduce neither the specialization gradient nor its attenuation.

detail.abstract: This article develops a systemic model of irritability as a predictable regulatory response to prolonged constraint, sustained uncertainty, and restricted agency. Irritability is conceptualized not as a dispositional trait, cultural norm, or individual deficit, but as a socially transmissible pattern of affective and behavioral regulation that stabilizes under chronic stress. The paper advances four original contributions. First, it formalizes a rigorous distinction between affective dysregulation and ethical failure, extending Viktor E. Frankl's insights beyond extreme conditions into ordinary institutional, familial, and civic environments. Second, it conceptualizes irritability as a transmissible regulatory pattern embedded in social roles, interactional routines, and stress physiology, explaining its persistence after coercive conditions have formally ceased. Third, drawing on long-term empirical observation and contemporary neurobehavioral research, it identifies specific behavioral markers through which constrained agency manifests across age groups and contexts. Fourth, the article outlines agency-preserving mechanisms that interrupt transmission without denial, withdrawal, or moral disengagement. The analysis integrates logotherapy, moral philosophy, historiography, systems theory, and neuroscience within a nonattributive, mechanism-focused framework. Implications are offered for leadership, institutional design, family systems, and resilience-oriented reform.

Stablecoins—digital tokens backed by fiat currency and high-quality liquid assets—represent an important step in the modernization of payment and settlement systems. When governed by clear prudential standards, they hold the potential to enhance payment efficiency, liquidity management, and transparency across the financial system. The GENIUS Act establishes an initial regulatory framework for stablecoin issuance in the United States by mandating full reserve backing, enforceable redemption rights, and standardized disclosures—features that aim to align stablecoin activity with long-standing financial stability and consumer protection objectives.

Despite concerns expressed in popular press or casual industry reports, empirical evidence and recent theoretical studies indicate that, under such a framework, stablecoins may complement rather than disrupt the traditional banking system. Deposit erosion or systemic risks depend critically on underlying economic frictions—particularly deposit-rate stickiness, search costs, and reserve composition—and available evidence suggests that these risks appear limited under the new regulatory landscape. To date, stablecoin adoption has not produced meaningful aggregate outflows from traditional bank deposits. Moreover, under realistic yield environments consistent with the GENIUS Act, competition from regulated stablecoin issuers may reinforce rather than weaken bank intermediation by encouraging more competitive deposit pricing and more efficient liquidity allocation, provided that regulatory capital frameworks ensure a level playing field between tokenized liabilities and traditional deposits.

Stablecoins also present potential operational and strategic opportunities for incumbent financial institutions. Banks may derive benefits from providing custody and reserve-management services for issuers, managing associated high-quality liquid assets, or developing tokenized liabilities within prudential constraints. Integrating these functions—either directly or through partnerships with stablecoin issuers—may allow institutions to adapt existing business models to a broader, more digital ecosystem while maintaining customer relationships and operational continuity.

Importantly, the GENIUS Act’s safeguards are poised to address the key vulnerabilities identified in the literature, including run and liquidity risk. Full one-to-one backing in high-quality liquid assets (cash, Treasury bills, and deposits at insured depositories), legally enforceable par-value redemption rights, and standardized public disclosure of reserves reduce uncertainty about issuers’ solvency and liquidity, thereby lowering the likelihood of run-like redemption pressures. As adoption grows and markets for stablecoins deepen, broader institutional participation and reputation effects may further support peg stability in normal market conditions. Stablecoins may also support financial stability more broadly: their demand for safe assets can deepen these markets, and under stress, regulated stablecoins may channel flows toward high-quality liquid assets, subject to the absorption capacity of Treasury markets. In addition, tokenized, on-chain settlement can improve operational resilience and reduce counterparty risk, particularly in cross-border transactions.

Looking ahead, collaboration between regulators, financial institutions, and technology providers will remain critical for ensuring that innovation proceeds within a safe and transparent framework. Naturally, residual risks remain, as no policy framework can eliminate them entirely. For example, reserve-only regimes remain exposed to extreme but low-probability shocks to safe-asset markets and to operational failures at custodial institutions. However, these vulnerabilities appear broadly comparable to those faced by other financial institutions and financial innovations in the past. Careful regulatory designs, not outright bans without a thorough understanding of the underlying economics, are needed.

Overall, with prudent oversight, issuer diversification, and consistent global standards, well-regulated stablecoins can serve as a durable, interoperable payment instrument integrated into the existing financial system, advancing its infrastructure, inclusion, and resilience in both theory and practice.

title: Gauging Hourly Economic Activity in Your Neighborhood
affiliations: University of California San Diego, UCSD  and

detail.title: Gauging Hourly Economic Activity in Your Neighborhood
detail.abstract: Imagine gauging hourly economic activity at the local (zip-code) level. We argue that this is now feasible and propose a new granular economic modeling approach (GEM) for measuring, modeling, and predicting economic activity at high levels of granularity. Our approach uses bridging equations and aggregation constraints to link highly granular spatio-temporal data on variables such as foot traffic, traffic flows, electricity usage and credit card spending with aggregate data on payrolls and income. We extract a common dynamic factor that summarizes local, hourly economic activity and is consistent with observable measures observed at far coarser levels of granularity such as city-wide payroll data and GDP.

title: The Impact of Overtourism in Cultural Resilience in Badung, Bali: Commercialization of Culture
affiliations: Universitas Pendidikan Nasional, Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM) and University of Gadjah Mada

detail.title: The Impact of Overtourism in Cultural Resilience in Badung, Bali: Commercialization of Culture
detail.abstract: This research examines how overtourism affects the cultural resilience of local communities, especially in relation to social practices, traditional values, and cultural identity in Badung, Bali. This study used a qualitative method involving interviews with 25 people, field observations, literature reviews, and thematic coding for data analysis. The research findings indicate that excessive tourism is impacting cultural resilience in Badung, Bali, leading to its commercialization. This excessive commercialization involves shifts in social values, dynamic cultural characteristics, the commitment of local governments, and the role of traditional villages. The study concludes that while excessive tourism poses substantial problems, the cultural resilience of the Badung community remains flexible and adaptive, shaped by ongoing efforts to balance economic demands with the preservation of cultural authenticity.

title: Legitimate Extraction: Sophisticated Laundering Hides in Plain Sight Hedging as the Fourth Money Laundering Stage

detail.title: Legitimate Extraction: Sophisticated Laundering Hides in Plain Sight Hedging as the Fourth Money Laundering Stage

keywords: petrostate corruption JEL Codes: G28 (Government Policy and Regulation)
K42 (Illegal Behavior and Enforcement of Law)

detail.abstract:
The architecture of anti-money laundering regulation reveals something curious when examined closely: the frameworks designed to combat illicit finance have, over decades, become quite effective at detecting the primitive methods—cash structuring, money mules, the deposit patterns that first emerged during Prohibition—while remaining largely blind to the sophisticated mechanisms through which the most consequential wealth extraction actually occurs. This paper examines that asymmetry through five cases spanning different decades and regulatory environments (BCCI, the London Laundromat, Danske Bank, FTX, and Binance), and finds that what appears as regulatory gap is better understood as regulatory architecture—a structure that, by design or by accident, directs attention toward certain kinds of transactions while leaving others invisible.

The traditional three-stage model of money laundering—placement, layering, integration—describes cash-based crime elegantly, but it rests on assumptions that fail when we turn from drug traffickers to kleptocratic elites: that illicit funds must be smuggled into the financial system, that their origins carry markers of suspicion, that the objective is returning dirty money to the legitimate economy for consumption. What this paper proposes is the recognition of a fourth stage, hedging, in which extracted wealth is converted into precisely the activities that regulatory frameworks not only permit but encourage—currency hedges, commodity futures, the ordinary prudence of protecting assets against volatility. The same transactions that constitute responsible risk management can simultaneously serve as the final step in kleptocratic extraction, and this dual nature is what makes the hedging stage both distinctive and, under current frameworks, essentially undetectable.

Drawing on evidence from the Panama Papers, the Pandora Papers, and court records documenting sovereign hedging programs, the analysis traces how these mechanisms operate in practice: the Kazakhstan devaluations where elites positioned offshore while citizens absorbed purchasing power collapse, the London property market where opacity serves insurance functions for the politically exposed, the derivative contracts where beneficial ownership disappears into offshore structures. The Vienna Convention (1988) and Palermo Convention (2000) define money laundering broadly enough to reach these mechanisms—the conversion of property derived from offense, undertaken to evade legal consequences—but current frameworks do not operationalize this reach.

What follows is a set of proposals: transparency requirements for sovereign hedging programs, beneficial ownership verification for derivative counterparties, hedging transaction due diligence calibrated to actual rather than assumed risk profiles. None of this would eliminate the fourth stage, but it might begin to address the gap between what AML frameworks claim to combat and what they actually see.

title: Adverse Impact Indicators: How Sustainable are Sustainable Funds?
affiliations: Justus-Liebig-University Giessen,  and University of Giessen - Department of Financial Services

detail.title: Adverse Impact Indicators: How Sustainable are Sustainable Funds?
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates whether sustainable funds effectively minimize adverse impact, measured using the Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators. We confirm that both sustainable fund names and SFDR labels are associated with lower adverse impact. However, we still find impact heterogeneity across individual PAI indicators and only a weak distinction in impact levels between Article 8 and Article 9 funds. Notably, our analysis reveals that voluntary PAI indicators often possess greater predictive power with regard to impact than mandatory ones. We conclude that broad sustainability classifications such as fund names or SFDR labels alone are insufficient for impactfocused investors. Moreover, regulators should revise the designation of mandatory versus voluntary PAI indicators to better reflect the actual drivers of sustainability.

title: Heaven or Earth? The Evolving Role of Global Shocks for Domestic Monetary Policy
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, World Bank and World Bank

detail.title: Heaven or Earth? The Evolving Role of Global Shocks for Domestic Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: Business cycles are increasingly driven by global shocks, rather than the domestic demand shocks prominent in earlier decades, posing challenges for central banks seeking to meet domestic mandates and communicate their policy decisions. This paper analyzes the evolving influence and characteristics of global and domestic shocks in advanced economies from 1970-2024 using a new FAVAR model that decomposes movements in interest rates, inflation, and output growth into four global shocks (demand, supply, oil, and monetary policy) and three domestic shocks (demand, supply, and monetary policy). We find that the role of global shocks has increased sharply over time and that their characteristics differ from those of domestic shocks across multiple dimensions. Compared to domestic shocks, global shocks have a larger supply component, higher variance, more persistent effects on inflation, and are more asymmetric (contributing more to tightening than to easing phases of monetary policy). As global supply shocks have become more prominent, central banks have also been less willing to "look through" their effects on inflation than for comparable domestic shocks. The distinct characteristics and rising influence of global shocks-particularly global supply shocks-have significant implications for modeling monetary policy and designing central bank frameworks.

title: A Temporal Concentration Index for Credit Portfolios with Continuous-Time Markov Default Dynamics
affiliations: University College London

detail.title: A Temporal Concentration Index for Credit Portfolios with Continuous-Time Markov Default Dynamics
detail.abstract:
Concentration risk measurement in credit portfolios has traditionally relied on static indices such as the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, which ignore the temporal dynamics of default clustering. We introduce the Temporal Concentration Index (TCI), a dynamic measure that integrates continuous-time Markov chain absorption dynamics with severity-weighted loss flows.

The TCI admits a conditional expectation representation: it equals the expected loss-flow concentration at the moment of default, given default within a specified horizon.

We establish sharp bounds, prove five axiomatic properties (normalization, symmetry, monotonicity, continuity, convergence), and derive a decomposition separating flow-timing concentration from severity-induced concentration. Closed-form horizon sensitivity formulas yield an interpretable factorization into conditional default intensity and concentration gap components, while a second-order ODE characterization enables efficient computation.

We derive the Hessian matrix with respect to loss severity parameters, providing convexity criteria and a Taylor expansion framework for rapid stress testing. Extending to multi-obligor portfolios with correlated defaults, we establish granularity limits showing O(N^-1) convergence to a systematic concentration measure, and develop Euler-based capital allocation decomposing portfolio TCI into obligor-level risk contributions.

Two numerical case studies demonstrate practical applicability: the first yields TCI values ranging from 0.89 (6-month horizon) to 0.60 (10-year horizon), exceeding the static HHI by up to 54%, while the second exhibits a critical horizon at t*h = 2.65 years where concentration transitions from decreasing to increasing—illustrating the regime classification framework developed herein.

title: Competition Law in Times of Crisis Case Studies of the European Passenger Airline Sector and the Irish Beef Industry
affiliations: European University Institute, Department of Law (LAW), Alumni

detail.title: Competition Law in Times of Crisis Case Studies of the European Passenger Airline Sector and the Irish Beef Industry

publicationDetails.detailsText: Talbot, C. (2018). Competition law in times of crisis : Case studies of the airline sector and the Irish beef industry. Cambridge Scholars Publishing.

detail.abstract:
This book examines the role and utility of competition law within the EU’s legislative and regulatory dialogue, using its response to crisis conditions as a test of its aims and abilities. As such, its main conclusion is that competition policy acts as a forum for debate as to the direction of the European integration project, while competition law can serve as a tool for aiding in the implementation of broader policy objectives. The analysis here explores the role of the general economic context in the application of competition law, the existence of identifiable baselines applicable in crisis conditions, the ability and role of national competition authorities in applying competition law, and the ways in which the European Commission’s overarching policy goals can influence the application of competition law.

The decision to take an empirical approach to this research project stems from a conviction that an investigation into the real world situations faced by firms and consumers should underpin the evaluation of the applicable legal rules. Over the past number of years, the Commission has exerted more and more influence over the development of the regional and global airline industry, and this book identifies the emergence of an apparent overarching aim on the part of the Commission to create a market with a handful of ultra-competitive airlines with international reach serviced by an array of smaller feeder airlines on a regional basis. The study of Irish beef processing, on the other hand, identifies a high level of government involvement in providing the strategic thinking behind a crisis cartel scheme, and then demonstrates how the economic context exerted considerably more pressure on the government and the national court than on the competition authorities involved.

title: Paternalism After Behavioral Economics
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Paternalism After Behavioral Economics
detail.abstract: Is paternalism legitimate? Might it increase welfare? When would it compromise autonomy in some impermissible way? The outpouring of empirical work on cognitive biases, and on departures from perfect rationality, has led to a wholesale rethinking of paternalism and its limits. Over the last decades, three camps have emerged: (1) coercive paternalists, who urge that behavioral findings undermine John Stuart Mill's Harm Principle and greatly strengthen arguments for paternalistic mandates and bans; (2) libertarian paternalists, who urge that behavioral findings justify a host of paternalistic but freedom-preserving interventions or "nudges," such as warnings, reminders, labels, and automatic enrollment; and (3) antipaternalists, who urge that behavioral findings justify only, or at most, efforts to strengthen or "boost" people's competences, or their capacities to make good choices. On welfare grounds, it is possible to identify the assumptions under which one or another approach would be best. Libertarian paternalism often has significant advantages over coercive paternalism, at least in circumstances in which choosers are heterogeneous. But when all or most choosers err, the welfarist argument for coercive paternalism is strengthened. And when choosers are not only heterogeneous but also adequately informed and free from behavioral biases, antipaternalism makes a great deal of sense.

title: Belonging, Loss, and Reinvention: A Mixed-Methods Study of Indian Trailing Spouses in Thailand
affiliations: and Suresh Gyan Vihar University Jaipur

detail.title: Belonging, Loss, and Reinvention: A Mixed-Methods Study of Indian Trailing Spouses in Thailand

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article. The research was conducted independently and was not influenced by any commercial, institutional, or organisational interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was conducted in accordance with ethical standards for social science research. Participation was voluntary and based on informed consent. No personally identifiable information was collected, and all data were anonymised and securely stored in compliance with the Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) of Thailand (PDPA). The research involved minimal risk and anonymous participation.
